answers.java_tx_design: I haven't shipped a production Java service — my year so far has been on our ERP vendor's finance module, written in C# against a stored-procedure-heavy SQL Server backend. I haven't owned a transaction boundary decision there either; the core posting logic predates me and I've only added read-only reports on top of it.
answers.java_ops: Same answer as before — no Java, no Kubernetes work on my side. The ERP platform runs on a couple of Windows servers our infra contractor manages, so I've never had GC pauses or a connection pool to chase. I have restarted the report scheduler service when it hung, but that's the extent of it.
answers.rust_readiness: I haven't written Rust yet. My plan is to work through the official book and rewrite our report-export module as a side project first, since it's self-contained and I already know its logic. I'd budget about two months of evenings before I'd trust myself near anything production, and I'd want a narrow, well-defined boundary before touching a live path.
answers.rust_boundary: I'd start with something stateless and low-risk, not the ledger itself — maybe a single validation step that's easy to run side-by-side and compare against the existing output before switching traffic over. I'd watch for mismatches between the two outputs and only cut over once they agreed for a stretch of time. I don't have a real migration behind me to point to, though.
answers.money_correctness: I haven't built idempotency or retry handling myself. The ERP system doesn't take external payment callbacks — it's internal finance workflows — so duplicate delivery hasn't been something I've had to solve. I know the concepts from reading, but I can't give you a real incident of mine.
answers.incident_response: Six months in, a report I shipped double-counted refunds in one dashboard. I noticed the totals looked off during my own review the next morning, told my lead within the hour, and we corrected the query before the finance team used the numbers. Nobody else caught it first — I did, and said so.
answers.process_skipping: I haven't had a real production emergency yet, so I haven't been tempted to skip review. The one time I wanted to push a quick fix past our checklist, I asked my lead first instead, and we agreed to wait for the normal review since nothing was actually on fire.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: That refund double-count is the mistake I mentioned. I don't carry on-call yet — too junior for the rotation — but I do a weekly shift answering internal support tickets from the finance team, maybe five or six a week, walking through report discrepancies with them directly.
answers.evidence_decision: I pushed back once on a teammate's plan to hardcode a currency rounding rule instead of using the shared rounding utility. I ran both against a week of real transactions and showed three cases where his version was off by a cent. He agreed, we used the shared utility, and I didn't relitigate it after.
answers.own_contribution: In the refund double-count fix: I found the bug and wrote the corrected query myself; the decision to also add a daily reconciliation check was the team's, made in standup after I raised it. For the rounding disagreement, the three test cases were mine; adopting the shared utility everywhere else was a team call I didn't drive.
answers.java_recovery: I haven't restored data consistency in a Java service — I haven't worked in Java at all. The closest thing was cleaning up duplicate vendor records in the ERP database after an import script ran twice; I wrote a dedupe query, checked it against a count from the import log, and reran the report.
answers.java_perf_change: No Java performance work on my end. The slowest thing I've touched is a nightly ERP report that took eleven minutes; I added an index on the join column and got it to about ninety seconds, but that was SQL Server, not a Java service, so I'm not sure it answers your question.
answers.rust_hands_on: I haven't written any Rust yet, so I don't have a real stuck-on-ownership story to give you.
answers.rust_when_not: I'd guess the finance-heavy internal workflows, the things that change once a quarter and where nobody on my team knows Rust yet, shouldn't move first. I haven't held back a rewrite myself — I've never proposed one — so I can't give you a real example, only that reasoning.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: I haven't chased a reconciliation mismatch. The ERP work I do doesn't touch settlement numbers, so I don't have a real incident to walk you through here either.
answers.prod_data_verification: I haven't been tempted to check something against production data — I don't have write access to anything customer-facing yet. If I couldn't reproduce something in test, I'd ask someone senior before going near production data rather than doing it myself quietly.
